_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: All concede: even according to the Rabbis, who say that [an animal that was] lost at the time of designation grazes, they concede that if he drew one of them and sacrificed it on his own initiative, he has rejected the other with his own hands, for he has revealed his mind that he does not care about it. And even if he drew the lost one and achieved atonement with it, the remaining one, which was never lost, dies. Where the Rabbis disagree is with one who comes to consult, for he has revealed his mind that he wants a remedy for them: he designated a sin offering and it was lost, and he designated another, and the first was found, and he came before us to consult what to do; we say to him: Go achieve atonement with the lost one, and the one that is not lost shall graze. This too, that it teaches “from these and from those,” which implies that if he brought from one of them the second goes to the Dead Sea, even if he achieved atonement with the lost [money]: you find it, for example, where he drew on his own initiative and did not consult, for there the Rabbis concede. Therefore [the tanna] taught this remedy, “he brings from these and from those”; and this remedy suits him better than saying: Let him trouble himself to come to the court and consult, and we will tell him to achieve atonement with the lost [money], and that which is not lost shall go to gift offerings.
tosafot:a1.1: (All concede that if he drew one of them and sacrificed it) The first clause is Rabbi and the latter clause the Rabbis [so the printed heading; the Gemara says the first clause is the Rabbis and the latter Rabbi]: And if it is difficult: let him answer for Rabbi Abba too: What is “sacrificed”? [Brought near] for slaughter, and before the slaughter the first was found, so it dies; and it is Rabbi, who said that one lost at the time of designation dies, and the latter clause and the first clause are both Rabbi. That is no objection, for if so, why did he mention “sacrificed” at all? Let him teach simply “designated.” Granted, according to Rav Huna, he mentioned “sacrificed” to teach us “on his own initiative,” that he drew it on his own and did not consult. Rashi’s wording: “All concede that if he drew one of them and sacrificed it, the second dies; they disagreed only about one who comes to consult.” And if you say: how shall we settle the wording of the mishna according to Rav Huna, where we learned, “And the Rabbis say: A sin offering does not die unless it was found after the owner achieved atonement”? One can say that this is what it is saying: a sin offering does not die such that we cannot find a remedy for it, except where it was found after the owner achieved atonement, for then it has no remedy. And according to Rabbi Abba too we will explain the wording of the mishna this way.
rashi:a2.1: But according to Rabbi Abba, who said: even if he drew the lost one on his own initiative and achieved atonement with it, the Rabbis say [the other] grazes, since it was neither rejected nor ever lost, even though he did not consult; and it is about this that they disagree.
gershom:a1.1: But according to Rabbi Abba, who said that Rav said: below too, “All concede” [that if he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost, the lost one that remains dies; about what did they disagree? About where he achieved atonement with the lost one and the one that is not lost remained].
rashi:a2.2: For Rabbi holds that one who designates for a lost one, it is like the lost one: one who designates [an animal] in place of a lost offering, its law is like the lost one. Just as, if he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost, you concede that the remaining lost one dies, so too when he achieves atonement with the lost one, the one that is not lost dies.
rashi:a2.3: And the Rabbis hold it is not like the lost one: and that which is taught, “from these and from those,” implying that if he achieved atonement with one of them, even with the lost [money], the [money] that is not lost goes to the Dead Sea, is Rabbi and not the Rabbis. The first clause is the Rabbis and the latter clause is Rabbi.
gershom:a2.1: For Rabbi holds one who designates for a lost one: what he designated in place of the lost one has the law of the lost one; just as the lost one, when it remains, dies, so too the one that is not lost, if it remains, also dies. And the Rabbis hold one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one, [but if] the one that is not lost [remains], it grazes. And with money too: one who designates money for his sin offering and it was lost, and he designated other money in its stead, the Rabbis hold that [money designated] for a lost one is not like the lost one, and even though he brought from these and did not bring from those, the money that is not lost goes to gift offerings. According to Rabbi Abba’s reasoning, the latter clause, from which we inferred “but if he brought from these and did not bring from those, [what remained goes to the Dead Sea],” cannot be established according to the Rabbis but according to Rabbi: the first clause the tanna taught us unattributed according to the Rabbis, and the latter clause according to Rabbi. Yes.
gershom:a3.1: And what does it teach us with these unattributed clauses, that Rabbi and the Rabbis disagree? But it teaches explicitly in the latter clause that they disagree: “One who designates,” etc.
rashi:a5.1: This is what it is saying: this matter is a dispute of Rabbi and the Rabbis: the latter clause, which teaches the dispute explicitly, is saying this: it tells us that this matter, those clauses above which conflict with each other, is one Rabbi and one the Rabbis.
rashi:a5.2: The Jerusalem version [reads]: “This works out well according to Rav Huna, who said: All concede that if he drew one of them and sacrificed, whether he achieved atonement with the lost one or whether he achieved atonement, etc. What is the ‘sacrificed’ taught in the first clause, ‘and he sacrificed another in its stead’? He brought it near to slaughter on his own initiative.” And this is what it is saying: he brought another near for slaughter in its stead, and an unqualified “brought near” implies on his own initiative; and after he had brought the other near for slaughter on his own, the first was found while the other had not yet been slaughtered: this remaining one dies, even if he set this one aside and achieved atonement with the lost one, since he did not consult. And the first clause and the latter clause are the statement of all, for now one cannot infer from the first clause “but if he did not sacrifice, it grazes,” since we are dealing with a case where he did not [actually] sacrifice. And the latter clause too, which teaches “he brings from these and from those,” but if he brings from one of them the others go to the Dead Sea, is the statement of all, for unqualified, it implies that he sacrificed on his own initiative without consulting.
rashi:a5.3: But according to Rabbi Abba, etc., and the Rabbis hold it is not like the lost one: and [the other] grazes, even though he drew the lost one on his own initiative and rejected this one. Now one cannot answer the first clause, “What is ‘sacrificed’? Brought near for slaughter on his own,” for on account of drawing nothing is effected; rather, he certainly actually sacrificed, and one may infer: but if he did not sacrifice, the second grazes, where he achieved atonement with the one that was not lost; and it is the Rabbis, [who hold that] one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one. With money too, one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one. And the latter clause, which implies that if he brings from one of them, even the remaining money that is not lost [the printed text has a stray “(Ḥullin)” here] goes to the Dead Sea, is not in accordance with the Rabbis: the first clause is the Rabbis and the latter clause is Rabbi. And if it is difficult: for Rabbi Abba too let him answer, “What is ‘sacrificed’? For slaughter, and before the slaughter the first was found, so it dies; and it is Rabbi, who said one lost at the time of designation dies, and the first clause and the latter clause are both Rabbi”: that is no objection, for if so, why did he mention “sacrificed” at all? Let him teach simply “designated.” Granted, according to Rav Huna he mentioned “sacrificed” to teach us “on his own initiative,” that if he drew it to sacrifice and did not consult, they did not make a remedy for him.
gershom:a4.1: Another version: “This works out well according to Rav Huna, who said: All concede that if he drew one of them on his own initiative,” as we said, “and sacrificed, that the second that remains dies,” whether the lost one remained or the one that is not lost remained, [it dies].
gershom:a5.1: The latter clause, from which we inferred that [the money] goes to the Dead Sea, accords with Rabbi; and it also works out well according to Rav Huna, for one can establish the first clause too according to Rabbi. How so? One can say: what is “sacrificed” [taught in the first clause, “another in its stead,” and afterward the first was found? It does not mean literally (the bracketed text reads “designated”); rather, he brought another in its stead near] for slaughter on his own initiative [and did not slaughter it until his lost sin offering was found, and he achieved atonement with the lost one on his own. “The first shall die,” which it teaches, refers to that first one, which he brought near to slaughter before the lost one was found; that is why it calls it “first,” and it dies because] he drew one of them on his own initiative. And one can say that even the first clause is Rabbi, and one cannot infer from it that the reason is because he sacrificed, for “sacrificed” does not mean actually sacrificed but brought near for slaughter. But according to Rabbi Abba, who said that Rav said, “All concede that if he achieved atonement,” etc., the latter clause, as we inferred from it that [the money] goes to the Dead Sea, cannot be established according to the Rabbis at all, but according to Rabbi, who said one who designates for a lost one is like the lost one: the first clause is the Rabbis and the latter clause is Rabbi. Yes. And what does it teach us, etc.
rashi:a6.1: They did not make an ordinance with regard to consecrated items: we do not care if the second dies, and we say to him: Go achieve atonement with the one that is not lost, etc.
tosafot:a6.1: For Rabbi holds they did not make an ordinance with regard to consecrated items: My teacher [abbreviated HaRaMaR] found this astonishing: does one destroy consecrated items with one’s own hands, when it is in our power to remedy it? And he answered: for example, where there is gain in the matter, such as where the lost one is lean and the one that is not lost is fat, for we say to him: Achieve atonement with the good one, and the lean one shall die.
gershom:a6.1: The matter itself: Rav Huna said that Rav said: All concede that if he drew one of them and sacrificed it on his own initiative, the second dies, for we penalize him since he acted on his own. About what did they disagree? About one who comes to consult which one to sacrifice. For Rabbi holds they did not make an ordinance with regard to consecrated items, for we do not care about the one that dies; rather, we say to him: Go achieve atonement with the one that is not lost, in which no defect arose, and the lost one, in which a defect arose, dies. And the Rabbis [hold they made an ordinance with regard to consecrated items, so that it will not die, and we say to him: Go achieve atonement with the lost one, etc.].
rashi:a6.2: And the Rabbis hold, etc.: and this is how the mishna is to be understood: “One of them shall be sacrificed and the second shall die,” that the one that is not lost is sacrificed and the lost one dies, “the statement of Rabbi. And the Rabbis say: A sin offering does not die” in a case like this, where he comes to consult, for we say to him: Achieve atonement with the lost one; “but rather” that one which was found after the owner achieved atonement certainly dies, for there is no remedy by consulting; and the same applies if it was found before and he did not consult.
gershom:a7.1: And this is how they disagree in the mishna, about one who comes to consult: Rabbi, who said it dies, holds that even though it was lost at the time of designation and not at the time of atonement, even so it dies, even though he comes to consult. And the Rabbis hold that if he comes to consult, the second never dies, and you do not find that it dies except for that which was found after atonement, [for in that case] he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost and the lost one remained; therefore it dies. [But] for one who comes to consult, the second never dies, because we say to him: Go achieve atonement with the lost one, because they made an ordinance with regard to consecrated items.
rashi:a7.1: They shall eat: concerning the remainder of the meal offering it is written (Leviticus 6:9): “And that which is left thereof shall Aaron and his sons eat,” and the end of the verse is “in the court of the Tent of Meeting they shall eat it.” He expounds “they shall eat it” as a superfluous verse, and says: “they shall eat,” without the letter heh: they eat non-sacred food and teruma with it, etc. And if it is difficult: but one does not bring non-sacred food into the Temple courtyard! This is not difficult: they eat them outside, and afterward they enter and eat the meal offering, so that it is eaten while satiated, as a proper eating.
tosafot:a7.1: They eat non-sacred food and teruma with it: And if it is difficult: but one does not bring non-sacred food into the Temple courtyard! That is not difficult: they eat it outside and afterward he enters and eats the meal offering, according to Rashi. And one can further say that it is prohibited to bring non-sacred items into the courtyard only when one performs some service with them, but for no purpose there is no concern; for here we see that a person enters the courtyard in non-sacred garments.
rashi:a8.1: They shall eat it: he expounds the heh of “they shall eat it” [yokhluha], which implies: they shall eat it alone.
rashi:a8.2: A large amount for consumption: that they have many remainders of meal offerings.
rashi:a9.1: What, is it not even Rabbi: and conclude from it that they made an ordinance with regard to consecrated items, for it teaches that they do not eat non-sacred food with it, so that it will not come to be notar and become disqualified.
gershom:a8.1: “They shall eat,” what does it teach? [And] “in the court of the Tent of Meeting they shall eat it,” what does it teach? For it is written: “And that which is left of the meal offering, Aaron and his sons shall eat; it shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place, in the court of the Tent of Meeting” [Leviticus 6:9], and it did not need to say “they shall eat” or “they shall eat it.” Rather, “they shall eat,” what does it teach? That if it was a small amount, if [the priest] had only a little of the meal offerings to eat, they eat non-sacred food or teruma with it, so that it is eaten from satiety, so that in eating it there will be satiation. And the heh of “they shall eat it,” what does it teach? That if he had much of the meal offerings, they do not eat [non-sacred food and teruma with it, so that the meal offering is not eaten in excess after satiation; that is why it is written “they shall eat it”: it, by itself]. And here, even though when it is much they do not eat non-sacred food and teruma with it, when it is little they made an ordinance that they eat non-sacred food and teruma with it; evidently they made an ordinance with regard to consecrated items. What, is this baraita not even Rabbi, since it is unattributed? And it is difficult for Rav Huna, who said that Rabbi holds they did not make an ordinance with regard to consecrated items. No, this baraita is the Rabbis.
gershom:a9.1: And Rabbi Abba said that Rav said: All concede, etc. About what did they disagree? About where he achieved atonement with the lost one, for Rabbi holds, etc. And this is how they disagree in the mishna: Rabbi, who said it dies, holds that even though it was lost at the time of designation and not at the time of atonement, and the one that is not lost remained, even so it dies, because one who designates for a lost one is like the lost one; even though it is the one that is not lost that remained, it dies. And the Rabbis hold that if the one that is not lost remained, it does not die, for a sin offering dies only if it was found after atonement; that is, if he achieved atonement with the lost one and the one that is not lost remained, it does not die, for one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one.
rashi:a11.1: The second shall graze: concerning the goats of Yom Kippur; and I explained it this way above (Temurah 22b).
rashi:a12.1: And Rav said: in tractate Yoma (64a).
rashi:a12.2: Living animals are not rejected: the first is not rejected by the death of its fellow, and it is sacrificed, and the second of the second pair grazes. And this latter one is like one who designates for a lost one, for they designated the two others because of the first one that died.
tosafot:a12.1: And the reason is that it is communal; but an individual’s dies. What, is it not according to the Rabbis: My teacher Rabbi Elḥanan found this astonishing: why does it not object directly from the mishna, which teaches, “And the Rabbis say: A sin offering does not die unless it was found after the owner achieved atonement”? Yet here both are present before atonement, and it says that an individual’s dies! And Rabbi Y. [abbreviated HaRaRY] says that it could not object from the mishna, for one can say that the mishna is saying this: a sin offering does not die except where it was found after the owner achieved atonement; but if it was found before atonement, both graze until they become blemished and are sold, and he brings a sin offering from these and from those. But with the goats it is not relevant to say this. However, it is possible that the Rabbis of the mishna hold that if he achieved atonement with one of them, even the lost one, the second dies, as here with the goats, where it is impossible to make another remedy: one cannot say that both graze and he brings from these and from those, since on that very day he must achieve atonement with one of them and cannot postpone the service of the day. But according to Rabbi Abba, who said according to the Rabbis that one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one, and that if he achieved atonement with the lost one the one that is not lost grazes, it objects well, for here he achieved atonement with the first, and even so an individual’s dies; evidently one who designates for a lost one is like the lost one. But for Rav Huna it poses no objection, for one can say that it is as when he drew one of them without consulting, where by right the second goes to its death in the case of an individual, even according to the Rabbis.
rashi:b1.1: What, is it not the Rabbis: and conclude from it that it is like the lost one; for he achieved atonement with the first, the fellow of the lost one, and this one, of which neither it nor its fellow was lost, would go to its death if they were an individual’s. Evidently the Rabbis’ reason is not this.
gershom:b11.1: And Rav said, disagreeing with Rabbi Yoḥanan: living animals in which there is no disqualification are not rejected, and when he achieves atonement, he achieves atonement with the second of the first pair, because living animals are not rejected; and the other, the latter one, the second of the second pair, is like one designated for a lost one, in place of the one that died, which is the lost one; and it teaches “it grazes.” The reason is that it is a communal sin offering; but an individual’s dies. What, is this mishna not even the Rabbis? And it is difficult for Rabbi Abba, who said that according to the Rabbis one who designates for a lost one is not like the lost one, and it grazes. No, that mishna is Rabbi and not the Rabbis. [His next words, on Rabbi Ami below:] Two piles of money as a guarantee: so that if one pile is lost they will achieve atonement with one.
gershom:b1.1: But if it was found at the outset, before atonement, it grazes, no difference whether he achieves atonement, etc. And it is difficult for both of them, both for Rav Huna and for Rabbi Abba.
rashi:b4.1: Of both of them: of Rav Huna and of Rabbi Abba.
rashi:b5.1: It teaches a matter that is absolute for it: that is to say, do not say “but if he did not sacrifice, it grazes,” for sometimes it grazes and sometimes it dies. For example, according to Rav Huna: if he drew and then sacrificed, even the lost one, the one that is not lost dies; if he came to consult, it grazes. And according to Rabbi Abba: whether he drew or consulted, if he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost, the lost one dies, and if he achieved atonement with the lost one, this one grazes. And the reason it teaches “sacrificed” before the first was found is that this is absolute for it, that it dies, with no distinction in the matter. And for this reason it did not teach “found before atonement, it dies,” establishing it, according to Rav Huna, where he did not consult, and according to Rabbi Abba, where he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost: because where it was found before atonement it is a matter that is not absolute, for it would need to set out a distinction as to which one grazes and which one dies. Another version: “But if it was found at the outset, it grazes: this works out well where he sacrificed the lost one,” etc.; and it is the same thing, except that it is the Jerusalem version.
gershom:b2.1: No, this is not difficult for them, for the tanna teaches a matter that is obvious to him. That is: one who designates his sin offering and it was lost, [and afterward the first was found] after atonement, it dies; this is obvious to him, and he teaches “it dies.” But this inference, “but if it was found at the outset,” he does not teach, because it is not obvious to him, for sometimes it grazes and sometimes it dies: for Rav Huna according to his view, that when he drew one on his own initiative the second dies and does not graze; and for Rabbi Abba according to his view, that if he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost, the lost one dies, even though it was lost at the time the second was designated and not at the time of atonement, even so it dies and does not graze. Since it is not obvious to him to teach “it grazes” always, he does not teach it; therefore it is not difficult.
rashi:b5.2: And let it teach “found at the outset”: that is to say, let it teach “found at the outset” and afterward “it dies,” and establish it, for Rav Huna, where he drew it, and for Rabbi Abba, where he achieved atonement with the one that is not lost.
rashi:b5.3: And it answers: It teaches a matter that is absolute for it, etc.
gershom:b3.1: Another version: “But if it was found at the outset, it grazes; this works out well…”: this version answers for Rabbi Abba. It works out well that you inferred “but if it was found at the outset, it grazes” where he sacrificed the lost one and the one that is not lost remained. But if he sacrificed the one that is not lost and the lost one remained, why does it graze? It dies, and it should have taught that.
gershom:b4.1: Rabbi Abba holds: when we infer “but if it was found at the outset, it grazes,” it is, for example, where he sacrificed the lost one and the one that is not lost remained; that is why it grazes.
gershom:b5.1: If so: that we are dealing with that case.
gershom:b6.1: Why does the mishna specifically teach [“he sacrificed and afterward it was found, it dies”]? Let it teach “it was found at the outset and he sacrificed,” etc., and all the more so “he sacrificed and afterward it was found,” that it dies.
gershom:b7.1: That which is not absolute for it, [that it] certainly dies, [it does not teach], for sometimes it dies and sometimes it grazes: if he achieved atonement with the lost one and the one that is not lost remained, it grazes; therefore the mishna does not teach it. But “he sacrificed and afterward it was found,” which is absolute for it, that it certainly dies, it teaches.
gershom:b8.1: We learned: One who designates money for his sin offering, etc.: [along the same course as we learned above, “one who designates his sin offering”]; and in another version it objects to Rabbi Abba alone.
rashi:b7.1: But [if he brought] from one: of them, he takes the second to the Dead Sea, etc. And it enters [the questioner’s] mind that it is the statement of all; evidently the Rabbis’ reason is not this.
tosafot:b7.1: But [if he brought] from one of them he takes them to the Dead Sea, etc., a refutation of both of them: It is astonishing: above it objected from this and said, “This works out well according to Rav Huna,” and for Rabbi Abba too it answered it according to Rabbi; and here it objects from it against both of them! One must say that [the questioner] now does not hold like the passage above; rather, it seems reasonable to the questioner here that it accords with the Rabbis as well and speaks of every case. And such is the way of the Talmud, to turn its question in every direction, sometimes this way and sometimes that.
gershom:b9.1: Rabbi Abba holds: when it teaches that they go to the Dead Sea, it is where he brought from the money that is not lost and the lost money remained.
rashi:b8.1: Here too, it teaches a matter that is absolute for it, etc.: that is to say, do not say “but [if he brought] from one of them, they go to the Dead Sea,” for sometimes they go to the Dead Sea and sometimes to gift offerings, for each Sage according to his view. And the reason it taught “from these and from those” and did not teach “he brings from one of them” is that it teaches a matter that is absolute for it, for this is certainly a complete remedy without any distinction; but had it taught “he brings from one of them,” it would have needed to distinguish, for Rav Huna, between drawing and not drawing, and for Rabbi Abba, between the lost money and that which is not lost.
gershom:b10.1: If so, why does it specifically teach, etc.: along the course above. [Come and hear: “The second”: this speaks of the two goats of Yom Kippur, where one of them died after he drew the lots, and he brought two and drew lots over them, as we said above: “The second shall graze,” etc.]
rashi:b9.1: As a guarantee: that if one of them is lost he will achieve atonement with its fellow.
tosafot:b9.1: One who designates two piles of money as a guarantee, etc.: If according to Rabbi, it is obvious. And below, regarding one who designates two sin offerings as a guarantee, it establishes it according to Rabbi and does not object “it is obvious.” For one can distinguish between one who designates money as a guarantee and one who designates animals as a guarantee; for here we see that even Rabbi Shimon, who says with regard to animals that it dies, concedes with regard to piles of money that he achieves atonement with one of them and the second “grazes” [i.e., is not destroyed].
gershom:b13.1: Another version: “It is obvious that according to the Rabbis they go to gift offerings, for now one can say,” etc. And rather according to Rabbi: according to Rabbi it is obvious, for Rabbi said that it dies only in one who designates for a lost one, but with a guarantee he concedes that they go to gift offerings [for there is no lost one].
gershom:b12.1: Is it necessary [to say this] as a guarantee: that the second goes to gift offerings?
rashi:b12.1: According to Rabbi Shimon: who said in the other chapter above (Temurah 15a) that five sin offerings die, and he does not hold of “grazes” at all, such that the money would go to gift offerings.
rashi:b12.2: Lest you say Rabbi Shimon does not hold of gift offerings: with regard to a sin offering, that just as he does not hold of it with animals, he also does not hold of it with money; it teaches us [that he does].
gershom:b14.1: Rather, it was necessary according to Rabbi Shimon, who said all five sin offerings die, [one of them] a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement. Lest you say that the second pile which remained should be like the surplus of a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement, and should die and not go to gift offerings, for Rabbi Shimon does not hold of gift offerings from the surplus of a sin offering, Rabbi Ami teaches us that he does hold of it.
gershom:b15.1: And can you say that he does not hold of gift offerings: from the surplus of a sin offering?
rashi:b13.1: New shekels [tiklin ḥadtin]: one who did not bring his shekel in Adar brings it all year and puts it in that horn; and when one of the three times arrives at which they take up [funds] from the chamber, they put them in the chamber, and it is taken up with the rest of the silver in the chamber.
rashi:b13.2: And on the second was written “old”: one who did not bring his shekel last year brings it the following year and puts it there, and from them they make the city wall and its towers and all the needs of the city; for [these] were made only from the surplus of the remainder in the chamber, as we learned (Shekalim 4:2): “The surplus of the remainder in the chamber: from it they would make the walls of the city,” etc. And this is surplus, for had it been there [in its year], it would have been left over.
rashi:b13.3: Pairs [kinin]: one who was lacking atonement, such as a zav, a zava, a woman after childbirth and a leper, who bring a pair of birds, brings money and puts it there, and eats consecrated food in the evening on the presumption that his atonement offering has been sacrificed; for the court of priests does not leave there until all the money in that horn is used up, so that one lacking atonement will not eat consecrated food.
rashi:b13.4: Fledglings for burnt offerings: on the fourth this was written; and one who donates young doves as a voluntary bird burnt offering brings money and puts it in.
rashi:b13.5: Wood: on the fifth was written “wood,” for one who donates wood for the arrangement [on the altar] brings money and puts it in.
rashi:b13.6: Frankincense: on the sixth was written “frankincense,” for one who donates frankincense casts money into it.
rashi:b13.7: And gold for the Ark Cover [kapporet]: one who donates for service vessels brings [money] and puts it in. Another version: “And gold for the kapporet”: one who donates service vessels brings and puts it in; kapporet means a basin, and in the book of Ezra it is written “golden bowls [kefori zahav],” etc. And for this reason it seems to me that this is the main [explanation], because things consecrated for Temple maintenance did not come to the Temple but to the hand of the treasurer.
gershom:b16.1: [But didn’t we learn: There were thirteen horns in the Temple, (and it was written) on them: “New shekels”: these were for the offerings of the whole year. “Old shekels”: one who did not give his shekel last year gives it now and puts it in that horn.]
gershom:b18.1: And fledglings for burnt offerings: these are young doves.
gershom:b19.1: Wood: with the money in that horn they buy wood for the needs of the arrangement [on the altar].
gershom:b20.1: And frankincense: for the purchase of frankincense.
gershom:b21.1: And gold: from which [comes] gold for the needs of the kapporet. And some say: gold for the kapporet, for the needs of Temple maintenance, for vessels overlaid with gold. The wording of my teacher, the Gaon.
rashi:b13.8: And six horns were for communal gift offerings that come from surplus: of sin offerings and guilt offerings, and all those of which we say “its money shall be allocated for gift offerings.” And in the last chapter of Menaḥot (107b) it explains what these six correspond to.
tosafot:b13.1: And six for gift offerings: In the last chapter of Menaḥot (107b) Amoraim disagree about what these six correspond to. Ḥizkiyya said: to the six priestly families [battei avot], so that they would be at peace with one another; therefore they instituted six, corresponding to the six weekdays, so that each family would have its day. And Ze’iri said: to a bull, a calf, a lamb, a ram, a kid and a goat. And why all this? Because they did not want to use the surplus of money for a bull for anything but a bull, and likewise for each one. And even though there is [one who says] in the first chapter of Shevuot (12b) that they use a bird burnt offering for the “dessert” of the altar, that is after the fact; but ab initio not, for it is better to use them for what they were originally designated.
gershom:b22.1: And six for gift offerings: for burnt offerings that come from the surplus; for the surplus from the money of a sin offering, a guilt offering and other offerings they put into those horns, and they buy burnt offerings with it.
rashi:b14.1: That its hide does not go to the priests: rather, they sell it again and buy animals as burnt offerings for the “dessert” [kayitz] of the altar.
gershom:b23.1: [And its hide does not go to the priests; the statement of Rabbi Yehuda: rather, they sell the hides and buy a burnt offering with their money.]
gershom:b24.1: [Rabbi Shimon said to him: If so, that their hides do not go to the priests,] he has negated the midrash of Jehoiada the priest. As it is taught: “It is a guilt offering” implies a guilt offering eaten by the priests, and it is written “a guilt offering to the Lord” [Leviticus 5:19]. How can these two verses both be fulfilled? [Rabbeinu Gershom names only Rabbi Shimon, where the daf says Rabbi Neḥemya, and some say Rabbi Shimon.]
gershom:b25.1: To include that which comes from the surplus of a sin offering and from the surplus of a guilt offering: that burnt offerings be bought with it, and the meat be entirely for God and the hides for the priests, and both verses are fulfilled. Evidently Rabbi Shimon holds of gift offerings from the surplus of a sin offering, and [Rabbi Ami] did not need to say it.
rashi:b16.1: In one set: for example, where he designated two piles of money for his sin offering, and lambs became cheaper, and some of the money was left over. [So the printed Rashi; Rabbeinu Gershom here speaks of a single pile.]
gershom:b26.1: It was necessary: it might enter your mind to say that when Rabbi Shimon holds of gift offerings from the surplus of a sin offering, that applies in one set, for example where he designated only one pile of money for a sin offering and some of it was left over.
